question: What does the k of five-pāda kan contribute independently, and which other grammatical traditions explain the Yama word?

operations: prescribe long ī for the original penultimate i
supply nām and retain its placement history
same_sense_histories.other_senses: See PG194 for the selected author and root entry. The associated farming sense is explicit in other witnesses, including Satyavrata.
same_sense_histories.evidence: PG187, PG194 and the printed 5.56 witnesses

operations: assign ī in place of the a of kan
attach the surface āśa of āśac
same_sense_histories.evidence: Daṇḍanātha Nārāyaṇa, printed p. 101, no. 749. The adjacent āśac headings establish the suffix string.

operations: admit the specified lexical formation under the paired headword rule
the commentary cites the root in the sense of knowing
retain the surface word as stipulated by nipātana
same_sense_histories.evidence: Durgasiṃha, printed p. 49, no. 246. The ensuing aṅkuśa sentence has a separate root and nasal comment. A productive intermediate chain for kit is not supplied here.

within_five_pada.result: The particular effect of k remains for investigation.
The m of nām fixes its placement after the last vowel, singled out in PG194.
His own gloss selects the affliction entry, and his footnote locates the augment after the last vowel of the root. He lists cultivation and Yama among the meanings.
The prescribed ī already accounts for the absence of guṇa. In his gloss he supplies “of the suffix” at the mention of the nām augment.
within_five_pada.scope: Record this wording alongside the root-placement account. It supplies neither a new independently visible operation for k nor a second worked segmentation.

scope: The three lexical histories map to the same unaccented Yama word under their own grammatical authorities. One cannot use the k of the Kātantra suffix or the āśa part of Bhoja’s suffix to assign a function to k in five-pāda kan.
